title: '95% chance the AMOC collapses': what the number means
summary: No study we read says there is a 95 percent chance that the Atlantic overturning circulation (AMOC) collapses before 2100. The widely repeated '95%' is the width of an uncertainty interval around an estimated collapse year in one 2023 paper, which was corrected in 2025 (current text: central estimate 2065, interval 2037-2109). The IPCC has medium confidence that an abrupt collapse will not happen before 2100, while weakening is very likely. Direct measurements at 26 N show strong variability and a decline since about 2010; they are not a forecast.

sections.heading: What the AMOC is
paragraphs: The AMOC is a system of Atlantic currents that carries warm water north near the surface and cold water south at depth. It is not the same thing as the Gulf Stream, which is wind-driven [a1].

sections.heading: Where '95%' comes from
paragraphs: Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen (2023) used North Atlantic sea-surface temperatures since 1870 as an indirect signal of the AMOC and extrapolated a trend toward a tipping point. In the current text the central estimate is 2065 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 2037-2109 [a2]. A 95 percent interval is a range for the year, not a 95 percent probability of collapse. The paper names no emissions scenario and assumes a steady drift; it says it cannot rule out other mechanisms [a2].

sections.heading: The 2025 correction
paragraphs: In August 2025 the authors corrected a code error that changed the tipping-time estimate by 8 years; figures, a table and estimates in the text were updated [a3]. The earlier coverage quoted about 2057, consistent with that shift, but the notice itself does not list the old and new values.

sections.heading: What other work says
paragraphs: The IPCC's sixth assessment has medium confidence that there will not be an abrupt collapse before 2100, and says weakening is very likely [a4]. A 2024 model study simulated a tipping event and argued the present AMOC is on a tipping course; its methods are debated [a5]. In 34 climate models forced by an abrupt quadrupling of CO2, the AMOC weakened by 20 to 81 percent (mean 54 percent) 90 years after the forcing but did not collapse; the authors conclude a twenty-first-century collapse (weakening below 6 Sv) is unlikely [a6].

A 2026 study (Portmann et al.) uses observations to constrain climate models and estimates a weakening of 51 +/- 8 percent (their 90 percent interval) by 2091-2100 relative to 1850-1900 under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, against 32 +/- 37 percent unconstrained. That is a weakening, not a collapse, and the authors caution that the interval rests on strong assumptions [a7]. A 2026 preprint on committed collapse is not peer reviewed and was not read [a8].

sections.heading: What is observed
paragraphs: The RAPID array at 26 N has measured the overturning since 2004 and shows variability from days to a decade, with a sustained decline after 2010-11 [a9]. The proxy used for the 2023 estimate (sea-surface temperature) is questioned by other scientists [a10].

claims.claim: 95 percent chance the AMOC collapses before 2100
claims.said_by: a video explainer; repeated in media
claims.source_says: Abstract: 'We estimate a collapse of the AMOC to occur around mid-century under the current scenario of future emissions'; the transition is 'most likely to occur around 2037-2109 (95% confidence interval)'. Maximum-likelihood method (Strang splitting): tipping year 2065, 95% interval 2037-2109. A second, moment-based method gives 2057. Table 1 (sea-surface-temperature proxy minus 1x, 2x or 3x the global mean): 2123 (2075-2288), 2065 (2037-2109), 2068 (2037-2101). The paper assumes its model is approximately correct, says 'we cannot rule out that other mechanisms are at play', does not exclude a partial collapse, and uses a sea-surface-temperature proxy. The 95 percent is the confidence interval of the estimated tipping year, not a 95 percent probability of collapse.
claims.verdict: unsupported as stated (an interval for a year, not a probability)
claims.source_title: Warning of a forthcoming collapse of the AMOC, Nature Communications 14, 4254
claims.read: full text opened (PMC10368695) and the corrected-publication PDF read by the PM (user-supplied); figures and supplement not read

claims.claim: The 2023 collapse estimate was corrected; 2057 and 2025-2095 are the earlier figures

The notice lists no old or new values.

claims.claim: A complete AMOC collapse this century is unlikely
claims.said_by: Baker et al., Nature 638, 987-994, published 26 Feb 2025 (corrected publication 2025)
claims.source_says: In 34 CMIP6 models forced by an abrupt quadrupling of CO2 held for 150 years, the AMOC weakened by 20 to 81 percent (mean 54 percent) 90 years after the forcing and 'does not collapse in the model experiments considered here'. In the seven models that also ran a 0.3 Sv freshwater experiment, the weakening was 50 to 80 percent in both experiments (means 56 and 61 percent). Southern Ocean wind-driven upwelling sustains the weakened AMOC; a Pacific overturning circulation emerges in almost all models but is too weak to balance it. Conclusion: 'a twenty-first century AMOC collapse (defined here as weakening to below 6 Sv) is unlikely'. The '90 years' are model years after the forcing in an idealised experiment, not calendar years.
claims.verdict: confirmed (full text read by the PM)
claims.source_title: Continued Atlantic overturning circulation even under climate extremes (Baker, Bell, Jackson, Vallis, Watson, Wood)
claims.read: full text read by the PM from the user-supplied PDF (21 pages); DS did not open the article

claims.claim: Observational constraints project about 50 percent AMOC weakening by the end of the century
claims.said_by: Portmann et al., Science Advances 12, eadx4298, 15 April 2026
claims.source_says: Abstract: climate models suggest 32 +/- 37 percent weakening by 2100 (90 percent probability, SSP2-4.5, CMIP6); the best observational constraint (ridge-regularized regression on 19 observed variables) gives 51 +/- 8 percent, about 60 percent stronger than the multimodel mean. Table 1 (SSP2-4.5, 32 models): constrained 2091-2100 AMOC 8.1 +/- 1.4 Sv against a constrained 1850-1900 reference of 16.4 +/- 1.7 Sv; weakening 50.7 +/- 8.3 percent (unconstrained 32.0 +/- 36.7). Constrained, other scenarios: SSP1-2.6 19.5 +/- 25.4, SSP3-7.0 48.4 +/- 5.0, SSP5-8.5 57.7 +/- 5.4 percent. 'Weakening' is the 2091-2100 mean relative to 1850-1900. The authors say the 90 percent interval 'does not rigorously represent a probability interval' and 'should be treated with caution' (models treated as independent and equally plausible, observation error neglected). RAPID 2005-2023 mean: 16.9 Sv. An estimate of weakening, not a probability or a date of collapse.
claims.source_title: Observational constraints project a ~50% AMOC weakening by the end of this century
claims.read: 16-page PDF read by the PM (user-supplied); DS did not open the article

known: Observed: RAPID 26 N array, 2004-2024, shows a decline since about 2010-11 and strong variability (rapid.ac.uk); the 2005-2023 mean transport is 16.9 Sv (as stated in Portmann et al. 2026).
Observed: North Atlantic sea-surface temperature records since 1870 (used indirectly in the 2023 paper).
forecast: Model-based, not observations: IPCC AR6 (weakening very likely; no abrupt collapse before 2100, medium confidence) [a4]; Baker et al. 2025 (34 models: weakening 20-81 percent, mean 54 percent, no collapse; collapse unlikely this century) [a6]; Portmann et al. 2026 (51 +/- 8 percent weakening by 2091-2100, SSP2-4.5) [a7]; Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen 2023 (statistical extrapolation: tipping year 2065, 95 percent interval 2037-2109) [a2]. These studies differ in method and in how close they put a tipping point.
unknown: Whether sea-surface temperature tracks the AMOC well enough to date a collapse.
How close the real AMOC is to a tipping point (models disagree and may be biased toward stability).
Whether the 2026 committed-collapse preprint holds up: not read.
